subject: humanities
passage: Many ensembles that specialize in historically informed performance play Baroque music with little or no vibrato, the slight, rapid wavering of pitch that most modern string players use almost continuously. These musicians argue that the constant vibrato familiar today became standard only in the twentieth century, and that eliminating it brings listeners closer to the sound that composers such as Vivaldi and Bach expected.
passage_b: Eighteenth-century violin treatises do not support the notion that Baroque players avoided vibrato altogether. Their authors describe it, often under other names, as an expressive ornament to be applied to particular long notes; what they warn against is using it on every note. Violinist and scholar Matteo Ferrandi concludes that a performance with no vibrato at all is as historically doubtful as one with vibrato throughout.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the approach to performance in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting that constant vibrato is unhistorical but doubting that none was used
choices.B: By arguing that Baroque violinists used vibrato on nearly every note they played
choices.C: By suggesting that the authors of the treatises disagreed sharply about vibrato
choices.D: By rejecting historically informed performance as an unreliable guide to Baroque style

explanation.why: The ensembles in Text 1 play with "little or no vibrato" because constant vibrato is a modern habit. Text 2 agrees that Baroque treatises warn against "using it on every note" but says they describe vibrato as an ornament for "particular long notes." Ferrandi therefore calls a performance "with no vibrato at all" historically doubtful too.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 agrees that continuous vibrato is not historical but argues that Baroque players did use vibrato selectively, so playing with none is also doubtful.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the treatises "warn against" using vibrato on every note.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 presents the treatises as agreeing that vibrato is an ornament for particular notes; it does not describe a disagreement.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 uses historical evidence to correct one practice; it does not reject historically informed performance as a whole.
